div.div: Catching 6 of 10 known faults says 'the method works', not 'it is better': the 95 % interval is 31–83 %, and it must be reported next to 4 of 10 pilot flags that were environmental (illustrative counts)
A. Building ground truth by hand [C1]
candidate cases (lab faults + resolved user reports)
usable: production-format log, right time range, identified bug, closed ticket
B. Detection rate with its 95 % interval [C1]

point = 60 % (my arithmetic). Ten cases give about +/- 25 pp; 100 cases at the same rate narrow it. The Wald interval is too wide at the top and misbehaves near 0 and 1. Ten cases cannot rank this method against one that scored 50 %.
C. Detection rate needs its false-alarm rate [C1]
detection rate (recall) = TP / (TP + FN); precision = TP / (TP + FP); false-alarm share of flags = 1 - precision. Flag everything and recall is 100 %.
forward pilot: 10 tickets [7*], of which 4 [8*] environmental
environmental = the customer's access point or internet, not the device [C4]. Confirm with a second signal before a ticket.

Backward validation [C1]: start from a known fault, find the snippet, check the detector flags the same device and window. Record: what, when, caught?, if not why and is it fixable. Necessary, not sufficient.

Forward pilot [C1]: a few cases a week to domain experts with no prior answer. Ask in order: is the output enough to start? what is missing? was the right anomaly flagged? Speed the cycle with a historical set and time-ordered cross-validation (train early, validate later, roll forward).

The misses name the missing signals [C1, C4]: Wi-Fi disconnects caused by the DHCP client; 'cannot register' caused by failed time sync; reboots from a kernel-driver assertion (kernel buffer); a log that ends at the crash; stateful order-dependent faults (need sequences). Fixable misses become the roadmap.

Legend — green = caught / Wilson interval / forward step; grey dashed = Wald interval; blue = usable cases, the 100-case interval and device-fault tickets; red dashed = false alarms (environmental); amber = misses. Circle = point estimate.

Sources — every number is loaded from ../constants.json. [n] = public (real value, cited); [n*] = illustrative (an invented round number of realistic order of magnitude; never a measurement). Wilson interval: Wilson, JASA 1927; NIST e-Handbook §7.2.4.1. Precision/recall as in Du et al., DeepLog, CCS 2017, §5.1.
[1*] ground_truth_candidates = 60 cases — illustrative
[2*] ground_truth_usable = 10 cases — illustrative
[3*] ground_truth_detected = 6 cases — illustrative
[4*] detection_rate_wilson95_6of10 = 31–83 % — illustrative; my arithmetic: Wilson score interval for 6/10 (illustrative counts)
[5*] detection_rate_wald95_6of10 = 30–90 % — illustrative; my arithmetic: normal (Wald) interval for 6/10, clipped/rounded (illustrative counts)
[6*] detection_rate_wilson95_60of100 = 50–69 % — illustrative; my arithmetic: Wilson score interval for 60/100 (illustrative counts)
[7*] pilot_tickets = 10 tickets — illustrative
[8*] pilot_environmental = 4 tickets — illustrative
